topics.title: One Rod Change Doubled the Load on This Walkway

demand.family: Bridge, dam or building: every corner cut

topics.hook: Hundreds were dancing in the hotel atrium. Above them hung two walkways on thin steel rods.
cause_chain: The original design hangs the 4th- and 2nd-floor walkways from one continuous rod per hanger
Even that connection reaches only about 60% of what the building code expected
During construction the fabricator asks, by phone, to switch to two offset rods; the change goes through without full checks
The 4th-floor box beams now carry both walkways, roughly double the load; during a tea dance the connections pull through
topics.rule_after: NBS BSS 143 (1982); the engineers lost their licences, and the profession made the structural engineer of record responsible for connection design and shop-drawing review.
topics.human_moment: Rescuers worked through the night to free people trapped under the fallen walkways.
topics.angle: Open at the moment of failure with a date/place/speed caption, cut back, walk the cause chain step by step with the physics, hold the toll for a turn, end on the rule that changed (named and dated).
topics.why_now: First batch (advice.md topic kinds and shares); settled event with an official report.

verify: Death toll: the NBS report and NIST page say 113 dead (later counts say 114); the script uses the report's 113

Phone request: ASCE Civil Engineering (Jan 2007) says the fabricator requested approval of the double-rod system by telephone and the engineer verbally approved; the engineering firm disputed receiving the call, so it is tagged 'as reported'

Added by studio 2026-11-22 from the NBS report (exec summary pp. v-vii, ch. 3 timeline p. 33, sec. 5.3.2, 10.3, 10.5) and ASCE Civil Engineering Jan 2007 (opened July 1980); Missouri board revoked two engineers' licences for gross negligence and misconduct (ASCE Civil Engineering July 2011)
outline: Hook (0-45 s): the atrium full on 17 Jul 1981, two stacked walkways on roof rods; 7:05 the upper one gives way onto the lower and both fall; steel and workmanship were not the cause (NBS conclusion 9); promise: a weak detail, a rod change, a review that missed it
1 The hotel: opened 1980; glass atrium; three walkways (2nd/4th stacked, 3rd offset), no columns, hung on rods; dance event, crowd 1,500-2,000 at 7:00 PM

2 The design: box beam = two 8-inch channels welded toe to toe; rod through the beam, washer and nut under it; one continuous rod roof-4th-2nd; even this would reach ~60% of the code's expected capacity

3 The change: fabricator's shop drawings use two rods, the lower set offset 4 in; request by phone, approved verbally (as reported; the firm disputed it); stamped as reviewed; the 4th-floor connection's load essentially doubled

4 The last minutes (MissionClock): 7:00 crowd; 63 people on the 2nd/4th walkways (news videotape); 7:04 band back for the dance contest; max load only 31% of the code-expected capacity; from day one barely able to carry their own weight

5 The failure (3D hero cutaway): connection 9UE, east end of the 4th-floor middle box beam; flanges rotate, lower weld splits, rod pulls through; neighbours fail; 4th drops onto 2nd, both fall; 7:08 first call; 113 dead, 186 injured (one beat)

6 The findings: NBS arrives 21 Jul; weighed spans (dead load ~8% over nominal), lab mock-ups; 302 kN expected vs 83 kN average; two factors; with the original rods the 3rd-floor walkway (53%) would have been weakest

7 What changed: Missouri board revoked two engineers' licences (gross negligence, misconduct); ASCE Oct 1985 policy: the engineer of record is responsible for all steel design including connections; payoff: they fell at 31% of what the code expected; ask: which link should have been caught first?
